strengths: Clear and well-motivated theoretical framing grounded in the Linear Representation Hypothesis, decomposing key and residual vectors into edit-relevant and edit-irrelevant subspaces.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three diverse model families (LLaMA-3-8B, GPT-J-6B, Qwen2.5-7B) and two benchmarks (CounterFact, zsRE), with substantial gains in specificity over strong baselines like AlphaEdit while largely preserving efficacy.

Extensive and thoughtful analysis section that empirically validates the core hypotheses (variance analysis of Ks/K⊥s, proportion of update affecting entity-agnostic components, steering experiments decomposing δ into w1/w2 components), going beyond simple end-task metrics.

Additional robustness checks, including a 5,000-edit sequential editing scalability test, contextual robustness evaluation on CHED, and token-level perturbation visualizations (heatmaps) that intuitively support the claim of reduced perturbation at the entity's last token.

Thorough ablation and hyperparameter tradeoff study isolating the contributions of the key-vector and residual-vector components, plus extensive baseline comparisons in the appendix (ROME, RECT, PRUNE, NSE, etc.).
weaknesses: Some core design choices appear heuristic and under-justified, e.g., the restriction of the residual update to a fixed 2-dimensional subspace (w1, w2) and the explicit assumption of zero interaction between these directions, which the authors themselves show is only approximately true (Figure 4/7 shows w1 also suppresses o and w2 also promotes o*).

Mixed results on General Capability (GC): SUIT underperforms AlphaEdit on GC for GPT-J (17.8 vs 19.51) and Qwen (23.7 vs 28.14) in the detailed per-benchmark table, which weakens the paper's claim that SUIT better preserves general capabilities across all settings.

Specificity/generalization gains are not uniformly positive — e.g., on zsRE for Qwen, SUIT's specificity (76.9) is notably lower than AlphaEdit's (86.3), and Table 1's headline '43.2-point' improvement is drawn from a single best-case setting rather than being representative of all conditions.

The entity-agnostic subspace K⊥s is computed once from a fixed sample of 10,000 PARAREL subjects; there is limited investigation of how sensitive results are to this subspace's stability across domains, subject types, or when applied outside factual-recall style data.

Incremental novelty: the core idea of restricting weight updates to task/edit-relevant subspaces is conceptually similar to existing null-space/subspace-constrained editing methods (e.g., AlphaEdit's null-space projection) and general linear representation/steering literature; the specific combination is useful but the individual techniques are largely adaptations of known ideas.

No reported variance or repeated runs across random seeds/edit orderings, making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of the reported gains, especially given some metrics (e.g., specificity) show high variability across models/datasets.

strengths: The paper is grounded in a clear conceptual motivation (Linear Representation Hypothesis) and proposes an intuitively appealing idea: constrain key/value updates to edit-relevant subspaces rather than the full activation space.
Extensive experimentation across three model families (LLaMA-3-8B, GPT-J-6B, Qwen2.5-7B) and two datasets (COUNTERFACT, ZSRE), with both generation-based and probability-based evaluation criteria.

A reasonably thorough analysis section attempts to validate the method's core hypotheses (variance analysis of Ks vs K_s^perp, steering experiments for w1/w2, proportion of update leaking into entity-agnostic subspace), which is a nice attempt at mechanistic justification beyond aggregate metrics.
Includes scalability experiments (5,000 sequential edits), robustness checks on a contextual dataset (CHED), and ablation/hyperparameter tradeoff studies, showing an effort toward completeness.
weaknesses: The core simplifying assumption behind the residual-vector method—that the edit-relevant subspace is exactly two-dimensional and that w1, w2 are orthogonal/non-interacting—is not theoretically justified and is directly contradicted by the paper's own analysis in Section 6.2.2 and Appendix G, which shows w1 and w2 are not actually disentangled (w1 also suppresses o, w2 also promotes o*). This undermines the stated mechanistic interpretation of the method.

Results are inconsistent across models: on GPT-J and Qwen2.5, SUIT frequently underperforms AlphaEdit on Specificity and/or General Capability (e.g., zsRE Specificity 89.5 vs 92.4 on GPT-J, 76.9 vs 86.3 on Qwen; GC 37.4 vs 41.0 on Qwen), which weakens the claim of a uniformly 'dramatic' improvement and suggests the strong headline number (LLaMA CounterFact +43.2 specificity) may not generalize.

The General Capability evaluation appears noisy and possibly unreliable — GPT-J and Qwen GC/MMLU numbers are erratic and occasionally near-zero or inconsistent across methods (e.g., Table 8), raising concerns about whether this benchmark suite is a trustworthy signal of side effects rather than measurement artifact.

The key hyperparameters (τ_energy=0.4, λ=0.3) are fixed identically across three quite different model architectures despite the paper's own tradeoff analysis (Fig. 5) showing substantial sensitivity of generalization/specificity to these values; no justification or per-model tuning/ablation is given for why one fixed setting should be optimal for all models.

The entity-agnostic subspace K_s^perp is estimated from 10,000 PARAREL subjects and then applied uniformly to COUNTERFACT/ZSRE edits without an analysis of distribution shift or out-of-domain generalization of this subspace.

No computational cost/runtime comparison is provided; the added SVD computation over 10k subjects plus the two-parameter residual optimization likely introduces nontrivial overhead relative to MEMIT/AlphaEdit, but this tradeoff is never quantified.

Results are reported as single-run point estimates throughout (Tables 1, 5, 6, 7, etc.) with no variance, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds, making it hard to assess whether the reported gains (especially the more modest ones on GPT-J/Qwen) are statistically meaningful.

The perturbation-reduction claims in Section 6.1, while visually suggestive (Fig. 2, 3), rely on a small number of qualitative heatmap examples (5 Wikinews articles) rather than a systematic quantitative benchmark of last-token perturbation across a large sample.

The ablation study (Table 5) is limited to a single dataset/model configuration and a single hard-coded hyperparameter setting, providing relatively thin evidence for the claimed 'powerful synergy' between the two components beyond the specific point compared.

strengths: The paper is grounded in a clear theoretical motivation (Linear Representation Hypothesis) and proposes a coherent method (SUIT) that decomposes both key and residual vectors into edit-relevant and edit-irrelevant subspaces.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three different model families (LLaMA-3-8B, GPT-J-6B, Qwen2.5-7B) and two benchmarks (CounterFact, zsRE), showing large and consistent gains in Specificity over strong baselines (especially AlphaEdit) while maintaining competitive Efficacy/Generalization.

Thorough set of validation analyses: variance analysis of entity-specific vs entity-agnostic key components, measurement of how much the update matrix leaks into the entity-agnostic subspace, steering experiments decomposing the residual vector into critical/non-critical directions, and last-token perturbation visualizations across multiple sample articles.

Good robustness checks: 5,000-edit sequential setting tracking general capability degradation over time, evaluation on the CHED contextual robustness dataset, and both generation-based and probability-based evaluation criteria.

Reasonably strong reproducibility support: detailed appendix with closed-form derivations (AlphaEdit formula, additive update derivation), full hyperparameter settings, and descriptions of all baselines and metrics.
Ablation study cleanly isolates the contribution of the key-vector constraint vs the residual-vector constraint, demonstrating a synergistic effect when combined.
weaknesses: The 2D subspace assumption for the residual vector (w1, w2) is admitted by the authors themselves to not be fully disentangled (w1 also suppresses the old object and w2 also promotes the new object), which weakens the core interpretive claim of the method and is not deeply investigated theoretically.

Results are mixed on some model/metric combinations: for Qwen2.5 on zsRE, SUIT underperforms AlphaEdit on Specificity (93.9 vs 97.5); on GPT-J, SUIT has lower General Capability scores than AlphaEdit/MEMIT in several benchmarks (Table 8), suggesting the specificity/efficacy gains do not uniformly translate into better general-capability preservation.

The entity-agnostic subspace K⊥_s is computed once via SVD over 10,000 sampled subjects from a specific dataset (PARAREL) and applied uniformly; there is limited discussion of how sensitive this subspace estimate is to the sampling procedure, subject tokenization (single vs multi-token), or domain/language shift, which affects generalizability claims.

Key hyperparameters (τ_energy = 0.4, λ = 0.3) are fixed identically across all three very different models without deeper justification or sensitivity analysis per model, despite the tradeoff curves shown being derived only on LLaMA-3.

No discussion of the additional computational/preprocessing overhead introduced by SUIT (e.g., SVD over 10k keys, extra optimization for w1/w2) relative to baselines, which is relevant to practical adoption.

Some claims (e.g., 'this effectiveness confirms that SUIT successfully identifies the critical subspace for the edit') are somewhat circular, since improved specificity alone is consistent with but not sufficient proof of correct subspace identification; while additional analyses partially address this, the causal story remains largely correlational.
Absence of variance/statistical significance reporting across multiple runs or random seeds, making it hard to assess the robustness of the reported margins (e.g., the 43.2-point specificity gain).

strengths: The paper proposes a well-motivated and conceptually clean method (SUIT) grounded in the Linear Representation Hypothesis, decomposing key/residual vectors into entity-specific and entity-agnostic (or object-relevant vs irrelevant) subspaces, offering an interpretable mechanism for improving specificity in locate-then-edit knowledge editing.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three models (LLaMA-3-8B, GPT-J-6B, Qwen2.5-7B) and two datasets (COUNTERFACT, ZSRE), with strong and consistent gains in specificity (up to +43.2 points over AlphaEdit) while largely maintaining efficacy and generalization.

Thorough set of supporting analyses: token-level perturbation visualization, variance analysis validating the entity-specific/agnostic subspace hypothesis, decomposition experiments validating the w1/w2 directions, hyperparameter tradeoff study, and ablations isolating the contribution of the key-vector and residual-vector components.

Substantial appendix material addressing robustness: scaling to a larger model (LLaMA2-13B), 5,000-edit sequential setting showing reduced degradation in general capability, RippleEdits and CHED evaluations, pre-computation cost analysis, and cross-model consistency of the spectral/energy curves used to justify the shared threshold.
Good transparency about limitations, e.g., explicitly noting that w1/w2 are not fully disentangled and discussing complications in ZSRE specificity metrics with a corrected evaluation protocol.
weaknesses: The two core components (subspace-aware key vector via SVD-based common-subspace removal, and 2D residual subspace via w1/w2 optimization) are somewhat heuristic and rely on several simplifying assumptions (e.g., ignoring interactions between w1 and w2, fixed global energy threshold across all edits and layers) that are not deeply justified theoretically, only empirically validated post-hoc.

Some results are mixed or only marginally better than baselines: e.g., on GPT-J, GC score is roughly on par with AlphaEdit and lower than others in several benchmarks (Table 10 shows SUIT's GPT-J general-capability average is close to or below AlphaEdit/MEMIT on several sub-tasks), and Generalization sometimes drops relative to AlphaEdit (e.g., Qwen: 86.8 vs 91.6).

The construction of Ks/K⊥s relies on a fixed external sample of 10,000 subjects from PARAREL and a single global energy threshold tau_energy tuned per model; there is limited discussion of how sensitive results are to this external dataset choice or whether the entity-agnostic subspace generalizes to out-of-distribution subjects/domains beyond Wikidata-style facts.

The method introduces additional hyperparameters (tau_energy, lambda) and a costly one-time pre-computation (SVD over up to 10k-25k subject keys per layer, with pre-computation costs reported in the tens of minutes to hours in the appendix), which somewhat undercuts the efficiency appeal typically associated with locate-then-edit methods, though this is partially addressed by the N=10k trade-off analysis.

The interpretability claims around w1/w2 as cleanly separated 'increase o*' and 'decrease o' directions are weakened by the paper's own analysis (Fig 4/7) showing that w1 also suppresses o and w2 also promotes o*, indicating the entanglement is non-trivial and undermining the cleanliness of the proposed geometric picture.

The writing, while detailed, is dense and the empirical narrative sometimes over-claims consistency ('dramatically improves', 'sets a new standard') relative to the somewhat mixed results across all models/metrics (e.g., GC scores, Generalization trade-offs).
